scenes.purpose: Open on the claim under test in the President's own words.

visual.description: Quote card: the four words type on in large type; 'inflation' lands last and holds.

citations.label: Donald Trump, Kalispell, Montana rally, Oct 2026

scenes.direction: Cold open; the quote types on as it is spoken.
scenes.narration: At a rally in Montana this October, President Trump told the crowd that "tariffs don't cause inflation".

scenes.purpose: Set the stakes: if the claim is wrong, someone is paying.

visual.description: One title line; 'paying' punches in on the last word.

scenes.direction: Camera punch on 'paying'; hold a beat.
scenes.narration: If he is right, a tariff costs shoppers nothing extra. If he is wrong, somebody here is paying it.

scenes.purpose: Trump's answer to who pays: other countries.

visual.description: Quote card with Trump's words only; 'paying us' is emphasised as it is spoken.
onScreenText: "are now paying us hundreds of billions of dollars"

citations.label: Donald Trump, 2026 State of the Union (PBS NewsHour)

scenes.direction: Quote enters as Trump's words begin in the narration.
scenes.narration: In his State of the Union, Trump said who he thinks pays: countries that were ripping us off "are now paying us hundreds of billions of dollars".

scenes.purpose: The opposite answer: Americans pay.

visual.description: Quote card mirroring sc03; 'paid by Americans' is emphasised.
onScreenText: "A tariff is just a tax paid by Americans, not by Canadians."

citations.label: Patrick Boyle, YouTube

scenes.direction: Hard cut from sc03 so the two quotes read as a pair.
scenes.narration: On his channel, Patrick Boyle puts it the other way round: "A tariff is just a tax paid by Americans, not by Canadians."

scenes.purpose: Turn from the two claims to the evidence, starting at the border.

visual.description: Split field: the two quotes slide apart and the gap opens on the line 'Follow the cost'.

scenes.direction: Wipe on 'follow the cost'.
scenes.narration: They cannot both be right. So follow the cost, starting at the border.

scenes.purpose: Show the test: foreign prices with the tariff taken out.

visual.description: The New York Fed blog passage; the definition of the measured price is highlighted as 'tariff taken out' is spoken.

excerpt.highlight: exclusive of tariffs (i.e., foreign export prices)

citations.label: New York Fed, Liberty Street Economics, Feb 2026

scenes.direction: Slow push into the highlighted line.
scenes.narration: If foreign sellers were paying, they would have cut their prices to make room for the tariff, so economists at the New York Fed checked their prices with the tariff taken out.

scenes.purpose: The result: foreign sellers barely cut, importers kept 94 percent.

visual.description: Two tiles: the small foreign price cut lands first, then the 94 percent share borne by the U.S. punches in larger.

chart.title: Who paid the 2025 tariffs, January to August

points.label: Foreign price cut per 10 percent tariff
Share of the cost on the U.S.

chart.note: Import prices proxied by unit values; incidence on U.S. firms and consumers combined.

citations.label: New York Fed, who is paying the 2025 tariffs

scenes.direction: Tile two lands on '94 percent'.
scenes.narration: In the first eight months of 2025, a 10 percent tariff cut those prices by only 0.6 percentage points, which by the Fed's estimate left 94 percent of the cost with American importers.

scenes.purpose: Show the late-year shift is small: the U.S. share only slipped to 86 percent.

visual.description: Three horizontal bars by period; the November bar is highlighted on '86 percent'.

chart.title: Share of tariff cost borne by the U.S.

citations.label: New York Fed, who is paying the 2025 tariffs

scenes.direction: Bars grow in order; November punches on '86 percent'.
scenes.narration: Foreign sellers did start giving more ground late in the year, yet in November importers still carried 86 percent.

scenes.purpose: Pivot from the border to the shelf.

visual.description: The question types on, centred.
onScreenText: How much of it reaches the shelf?

scenes.direction: Question types on with the second sentence; hold a beat.
scenes.narration: But an importer paying at the border is not yet a shopper paying at the till. How much of it reaches the shelf?

scenes.purpose: How much reaches consumer prices: about a quarter.

visual.description: One big tile: 26 percent of the tariff increase passes to consumer prices.

chart.title: Tariff increase passed to consumer prices
chart.note: Measured relative to less-exposed goods, holding aggregate conditions fixed.

citations.label: Amiti, Heise and Weinstein, NY Fed Staff Report 1201

scenes.direction: Tile counts up to 26 as the figure is spoken.
scenes.narration: A New York Fed staff report on the 2025 tariffs estimates that consumer prices rise by about 26 percent of the tariff increase, roughly a quarter of the tariff rate, measured against goods less exposed to the tariffs.

scenes.purpose: Split that rise: over a third comes from goods made at home.

visual.description: One stacked bar: imported varieties 64 percent, made at home 36 percent; the home segment lights up on '36 percent'.

chart.title: Where the consumer price rise comes from
chart.note: Shares of the consumer price increase, not of the tariff.

citations.label: Amiti, Heise and Weinstein, NY Fed Staff Report 1201

scenes.direction: Bar fills left to right; home segment highlighted on '36 percent'.
scenes.narration: And not all of that comes from imports: 36 percent of it comes from goods made at home, because American producers pay more for imported parts, and with foreign rivals pricier, they raise their markups.

scenes.purpose: Timing: imports pass through in months, home-made goods take most of a year.

visual.description: A list built one line per sentence: not on day one; imports half in three months, all in six; made at home nine to twelve months.
onScreenText: Not the day it is announced
Imports: half after three months, all after six
Made at home: nine to twelve months

citations.label: New York Fed, how fast tariffs pass through, Oct 2026
Amiti, Heise and Weinstein, NY Fed Staff Report 1201

scenes.direction: Each line lands with its sentence.
scenes.narration: Nor does it arrive the day a tariff is announced. In the New York Fed's estimates, about half of the direct effect on imported goods is in shop prices after three months, and all of it after six, as retailers take a few months to pass on higher costs. The part that runs through American-made goods is slower still, taking nine to twelve months to work through supply chains.

scenes.purpose: Why firms spread increases out, in the survey's words.

visual.description: The New York Fed survey passage; the fixed-price contracts line, then the gradual increases line, highlighted.

citations.label: New York Fed business surveys, Jul 2026

scenes.direction: Highlight on 'a little at a time'.
scenes.narration: Firms in the New York Fed's business surveys gave their reasons for spreading increases out: some sell under fixed-price contracts they cannot change until they expire, and some raise prices a little at a time to avoid shocking customers.

scenes.purpose: Pose the second question: bump or lasting inflation.

visual.description: The question types on.
onScreenText: A one-time bump, or lasting inflation?

scenes.direction: Hold a beat after the question.
scenes.narration: So is a tariff a one-time bump in prices, or lasting inflation?

scenes.purpose: The price-level effect: peaked near 3 percent, forecast to ease to about 2.

visual.description: Two tiles: the February 2026 peak, then the August 2026 forecast.

chart.title: Tariff effect on the consumer goods price level
chart.note: Level effect, not annual inflation; August is a forecast.

citations.label: New York Fed, how fast tariffs pass through, Oct 2026

scenes.direction: Second tile lands on 'about 2 percent'.
scenes.narration: The New York Fed estimates the tariffs' effect on the level of consumer goods prices peaked near 3 percent in February 2026, and forecasts it to ease to about 2 percent by August after a Supreme Court ruling cut some tariffs, then edge up again with new tariffs on Canadian goods.

scenes.purpose: The inflation contribution peaks, then fades to around zero.

visual.description: One tile: 2.9 percentage points at the February 2026 peak, with the caption that it is forecast to fall to around zero by August.

chart.title: Tariff contribution to yearly consumer goods inflation
chart.note: Forecast to fall to around zero by August 2026.

citations.label: New York Fed, how fast tariffs pass through, Oct 2026

scenes.direction: Tile lands on '2.9'.
scenes.narration: Its contribution to the yearly rise in consumer goods prices also peaked that February, at 2.9 percentage points, and is forecast to fall to around zero by August.

scenes.purpose: The caveat: one-time can be drawn out.

visual.description: The survey passage with the 'drawn-out affair' phrase highlighted.

excerpt.highlight: a drawn-out affair, especially when the tariffs change frequently

citations.label: New York Fed business surveys, Jul 2026

scenes.direction: Highlight sweeps as the quote is spoken.
scenes.narration: But the Fed's survey researchers warn that "one-time" can be "a drawn-out affair, especially when the tariffs change frequently", with many firms spreading price increases across extended periods.

scenes.purpose: Answer the first question: mostly not foreign sellers.

visual.description: One title line answering who pays.

citations.label: New York Fed, who is paying the 2025 tariffs
Amiti, Heise and Weinstein, NY Fed Staff Report 1201

scenes.direction: Title lands on 'mostly not foreign sellers'.
scenes.narration: So who pays? By the Fed's estimates, mostly not foreign sellers: American importers carried the bulk of the 2025 tariffs, and part of that cost reached consumer prices, including for goods made at home.

scenes.purpose: State the limit of the estimates in the study's own words.

visual.description: The staff report's limitation paragraph with the exchange-rate and monetary-policy line highlighted.

excerpt.highlight: not account for the possible tariff impact on the exchange rate, the monetary-policy response

citations.label: Amiti, Heise and Weinstein, NY Fed Staff Report 1201

scenes.direction: Highlight on 'exchange rate'.
scenes.narration: What these estimates cannot give you is the economy-wide inflation rate: they compare goods more and less exposed to tariffs, and leave out effects through the exchange rate and the Fed's monetary-policy response.

scenes.purpose: Answer the second question: a step up, taken slowly.

visual.description: One title line.
onScreenText: A step up in prices, taken slowly

citations.label: New York Fed, how fast tariffs pass through, Oct 2026
New York Fed business surveys, Jul 2026

scenes.direction: Hold a beat before the takeaway.
scenes.narration: Within those limits, the tariffs look more like a step up in prices than lasting inflation, though a step that firms are taking slowly.

scenes.purpose: Leave the viewer two checks to apply next time.

visual.description: A two-line list built one line per sentence.
onScreenText: Did their sellers cut their prices?
Made at home: the better part of a year

citations.label: Amiti, Heise and Weinstein, NY Fed Staff Report 1201

scenes.direction: Each line lands with its sentence; hold the end card.
scenes.narration: Next time someone says another country pays a tariff, ask one question: did that country's sellers cut their prices? And when a tariff changes, don't judge it by next week's receipts; the goods made at home take the better part of a year to catch up.
